pull_quotes.text: It's a solid crime drama with a neat, high-concept premise, and some fantastic performances - Beforeigners is an addictive binge.
This high-concept Norwegian TV series that blends time-travel science-fiction with buddy cop and murder mystery actually works.

seasons.review_body: Beforeigners (Fremvandrerne) launched on HBO Nordic in August 2019 with a premise that immediately marked it out as one of the more original crime dramas in recent European television: people from different historical periods are mysteriously emerging in contemporary Oslo and must integrate into modern society. The central murder investigation - a Stone Age woman found dead, a case assigned to detective Lars Haaland and his partner Alfhildr, a Viking-era arrival herself - functions simultaneously as procedural and immigration allegory. All five English-language critics at Rotten Tomatoes gave it a positive review. Pajiba called it an addictive binge with fantastic performances. The Chicago Tribune noted its procedural fidelity while flagging that the high-concept premise was sometimes more interesting than the character development. The show's underlying commentary on how societies treat new arrivals - refugee camps, integration programs, discrimination - gave it a cultural seriousness that critics appreciated.

episode_reviews.review_body:
# Beforeigners S01E01: "Episode 1" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

A radio call comes in. “Sierra two-zero” answers with “Excuse me,” a polite little glitch that tells you the pilot knows its chaos has rules. The scene leads with procedure, while panic waits outside the door. A responder checks whether the caller reported the incident, confirms people have appeared nearby, and tells someone, “Okay. Let's stay nice and calm, all right? We're here to help you.” That line is the episode’s operating manual. The world is cracking open, and the first instinct is still customer service.

The premiere works because it treats the impossible as paperwork, radio traffic, scene control and one death that refuses to fit the form.

## The Apocalypse Gets a Case Number

The cleanest choice in the episode is also its driest joke: the impossible feeds bureaucracy. It creates new categories.

The opening crisis cluster runs on short, practical exchanges. Someone appears. Someone calls it in. Someone confirms location. Someone says stay calm. Then the scale widens. **Kelly** is thanked as reports confirm the phenomenon is happening all over the world, and the pilot makes a sharp structural move. It establishes the global miracle, then files it away as the condition of ordinary life.

That jump matters. After the “few years later” tag, the arrivals are no longer a one-night rupture. They have become a managed pattern. A night arrival update can describe things as “Nice and quiet,” which is a brutal little joke if the episode lets it sit. The event that once required calm voices and emergency control now gets logged like weather.

That is the pilot’s argument in miniature. A society can absorb even the impossible if it can name it, staff it and write a report about it. The hour’s sharpness comes from watching that confidence decay once death enters the frame. A category can make chaos look smaller. It cannot make a body explain itself.

## A Body That Refuses the Form

The Tjuvholmen death is where the premiere starts tightening its grip. At first, the case is a question of classification: “Deceased During Arrival” or “Jumper”? The line is ugly in the right way. One option turns the dead woman into collateral damage of a known phenomenon. The other turns her into a familiar urban tragedy. Either label would let the system keep moving.

Then forensics complicates that comfort. The cause of death is thought to be strangulation. With that, the episode shifts from event management to murder investigation, and the tonal change is earned because the earlier scenes have trained the system to prefer neat explanations. The death cannot stay inside the arrival paperwork. It pushes back.

The writing is strongest when it makes language do the policing. “DDA” is a sedative as much as an acronym. It tells everyone where the dead belong before the evidence has finished speaking. The case at Sørenga repeats that pressure: another DDA call, onlookers, possible trouble, assistance requested. The vocabulary is already in place. The responders know what box to reach for.

The premiere’s real engine is the gap between the label and the body. Once strangulation enters, the death stops being a symptom of the phenomenon and becomes an act. That is a smarter hook than a monster in the water, because it makes the supernatural frame answer to a human crime.

## Lars Gets Saddled With a Symbol

The plan to team **Lars** with the department mascot for the murder investigation is the pilot’s most openly procedural beat, and it does useful character work even in outline. A murder case needs competence. The department gives Lars competence wrapped in image management.

That phrase, “department mascot,” carries bite. It suggests a person whose public value may have arrived before institutional trust did. The pairing is a staffing decision rather than a grand philosophical summit, which is why it lands. In this world, integration is not only an ideal or a social debate. It is who gets put on which case and why.

The episode is careful about escalation. It avoids a speech about history colliding with the present and lets a murder assignment carry the weight. Lars is placed in a partnership designed to solve more than a killing. The department also appears to be solving optics, legitimacy and its own discomfort with the new normal.

That is good pilot architecture. The case gives the episode momentum, while the pairing gives the season a machine. One weak spot: the available beats make the partner dynamic more suggested than fully dramatised here. The idea has charge, but the hour’s most concrete energy still belongs to crime scene logic and witness testimony. The partnership feels planted. It has not bloomed.

## The Monster Is a Bad Answer and a Great Problem

Then **the witness** insists the sea monster was “Hafgufa” and claims it took the woman. The premiere could play this as comic relief, a superstition dropped into a police case so the modern detectives can roll their eyes. Instead, the detail works because it attacks the investigation from another angle.

The central contradiction is not whether the hour asks everyone to believe in the monster. The problem is that the case cannot dismiss the monster talk without losing access to what the witness believes she saw. The scientific framework wants a body, a cause, a timeline. The witness offers myth. The episode’s smart choice is to make those languages collide inside a murder investigation rather than in a lecture.

That is why the later willingness to present Hafgufa materials to the team matters. The move does not prove the monster is real. It proves the investigation has to understand the world the witness is speaking from. A belief can be wrong and still be evidence. A vision can be impossible and still point toward pressure, fear or memory. The pilot keeps that ambiguity usable.

The weakness is that the Hafgufa turn risks becoming the flashiest object in the room. Strangulation is the cleaner investigative turn. The sea monster is the louder image. The episode stays mostly disciplined, but the balance is delicate. Lean too hard into creature talk and the murder’s procedural bite softens.

## The Pilot Trusts the Desk Lamp More Than the Lightning Strike

What separates this premiere from a noisier version of the same premise is pacing. The dialogue density spikes during the first crisis, slows into administrative rhythm, then rises again with the murder assignment and witness interrogation. That shape is deliberate. The hour begins with immediate confusion, normalises the impossible through routine, then lets one case puncture that routine.

The long silence windows suggested by the episode’s rhythm also matter. They imply cuts, resets and scene transitions that let the world breathe between information bursts. A premise this big can suffocate itself by explaining too much. Here, the pilot keeps returning to process: updates, forms, calls, assistance requests, team assignments. The desk lamp beats the lightning strike.

That restraint is the reason the hook lands. The episode understands that “happening all over the world” is not automatic drama. Drama begins when a person dies and the official language cannot decide what kind of death it is. That is the hour’s spine.

The pilot is not flawless. Its world-building is more compelling than its emotional texture in the beats provided, and some human relationships arrive as functional arrangements rather than lived-in bonds. As an opening argument, though, it is sturdy: if the past walks out of the sea, the future will still ask for the correct form.

## The Verdict

“Episode 1” is a smart, controlled opener that turns a wild premise into a procedural pressure cooker. Its strongest move is refusing to worship the phenomenon. The arrivals are global, but the story finds its shape in one dead woman, one disputed classification and one witness whose monster story cannot be laughed out of the room. The case gives the pilot direction, while Lars’s assignment hints at a season built around institutional discomfort as much as mystery.

The hour’s limitation is emotional distance. The machinery is sharper than the people so far. Still, that machinery is built with purpose. A good pilot, dry in the right places, strange without flailing, and confident enough to let procedure crowd the supernatural.

verdict.one_liner: A controlled pilot turns global time chaos into paperwork, murder and one monster story that refuses to stay silly.

bollymeter.basis: 60% on Rotten Tomatoes from 5 critics. Reviewers found Season 2 less intimate and more procedurally conventional; the high-concept energy of Season 1 diluted into a less focused narrative.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 arrived in December 2021 to a noticeably cooler critical reception - 60% on Rotten Tomatoes from 5 reviewers versus the debut's perfect score. The show scaled up its production ambitions in ways that reduced the intimate texture of Season 1, and the narrative feels less focused, spreading across more storylines without deepening any of them significantly. The high-concept premise remains intact but Season 2 deploys it more mechanically than the first season managed. For those already invested in the characters - particularly the partnership between Lars and Alfhildr - it is a watchable if diminished continuation. The series ended after this season with the central mysteries partially resolved.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 2 scales up and loses the close-focus intimacy that made Season 1's premise feel genuinely fresh.
